newsitem.title: USA: Growth, safety and roads seen as Okla.'s '97 focus.
newsitem.headline: Growth, safety and roads seen as Okla.'s '97 focus.

text.p: Economic growth, safer streets and better roads should be Oklahoma's top priorities in 1997, Governor Frank Keating told state legislators during Monday's State of the State Address.
On the economic front, Oklahoma's focus should be "true reform" of its workers compensation system," Keating said, according to prepared remarks.
"Last week I joined legislative leaders in pushing for a significant 10 percent rate cut," the governor said. "But we aren't going to fix this problem a few percentage points at a time."

Oklahoma's workers' comp costs were the nation's ninth highest in 1994, seventh highest in 1995 and fifth highest in 1996. Though costs have risen, benefits paid to deserving injured workers have not, he said. While Oklahoma's system is the fifth priciest of states surveyed, its workers ranked 35 in real benefits.

"Excessive workers' compensation costs are nothing more than a tax on business, and it is time to give Oklahoma employers a tax cut while we craft a system that protects the truly deserving injured worker," Keating said.
Keating said Michelin's Ardmore plant employs one-tenth of the company's U.S. workforce, but accounts for a third of Michelin's workers' comp expenses.
He cited Senate Bill 730, which Keating said would "revolutionize workers compensation coverage in Oklahoma," while being fair to all parties.
Citizen safety is Keating's second key priority, he said. The first step is to repeal the early release law. The second is to pass a truth-in-sentencing measure, he said.

"Truth-in-sentencing will keep the worst offenders behind bars for at least 85 percent of their sentences," Keating said. "More importantly, it will keep those violent and habitual criminals out of our homes and neighborhoods."
Keating said his budget will request $46 million in additional funding for the state's Department of Corrections.

"A portion of that money must go to increase staffing at the operational level," he said. "The remainder should be used to lease additional private bed space to place inmates now, without excessive capital construction costs."

Keating said the state can create a prison system that works through wise use of growth revenues, without a tax increase, he said. The prison system will require "further substantial investment" in the years ahead, Keating said.
The governor urged legislators to consider a report by Mike Quinlan, former head of the Federal Bureau of Prisons, who assessed the system at Keatings' request.

"I urge your full consideration of the reforms suggested by the Quinlan report and the swiftest possible action on repeal of early release, approval of truth-in-sentencing and the increased prison budget."

Lastly, Keating urged legislators to "get serious about our decaying network of roads and highways." Over the years, Oklahoma has paid more in taxes than it gets back in federal highway dollars, he said.

"Hopefully, Congress and the President will move to correct that imbalance, but given the trend toward devolution of powers and responsibilities to the states, we must make our own investments in highways if we are to remain competitive."
Keating said he will propose an additional $56 million in highway funding this year to start underwriting "an ambitious $750 million highway bond program that will carry us into the new century."
The governor said he was heartened by the "broad legistlative support" the program enjoys.
Also in Monday's address, Keating called for swift ratification of a federal balanced budget amendment.

"All eight members of Oklahoma's Congressional delegation have voiced their support for a federal balanced budget amendment to the United States Constitution," Keating said, adding that the amendment may be sent soon to the states for ratification.
"We Oklahomans know the wisdom of a constitutional mandate for fiscal common sense. Let's send some Oklahoma values to Washington by being the first to ratify this vital amendment."
